claim: S3 has no minimum charge; its cost components are storage, requests and data retrieval, data transfer and transfer acceleration, data management and insights features, replication, and transform and query features.
question: What do you pay for in Amazon S3?

values.display: storage pricing, request and data retrieval pricing, data transfer and transfer acceleration pricing, data management and insights feature pricing, replication pricing, and transform and query feature pricing
no minimum charge

evidence.quote: Pay only for what you use. There is no minimum charge. Amazon S3 cost components are storage pricing, request and data retrieval pricing, data transfer and transfer acceleration pricing, data management and insights feature pricing, replication pricing, and transform and query feature pricing.

claim: The storage charge depends on the size of the objects, how long they were stored during the month, and their storage class.
question: What decides the monthly storage charge of an S3 bucket?

values.display: your objects' size, how long you stored the objects during the month, and the storage class

evidence.quote: You pay for storing objects in your S3 buckets. The rate you’re charged depends on your objects' size, how long you stored the objects during the month, and the storage class—S3 Standard, S3 Intelligent-Tiering, S3 Standard-Infrequent Access, S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access, S3 Express One Zone, S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval (Formerly S3 Glacier), and S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

claim: S3 Intelligent-Tiering adds a monthly monitoring and automation charge per object, and has no retrieval charges and no tiering charges when objects move between access tiers.
question: What does S3 Intelligent-Tiering charge that other classes do not, and what does it not charge?

values.display: monthly monitoring and automation charge per object
no retrieval charges, and no additional tiering charges

evidence.quote: You pay a monthly monitoring and automation charge per object stored in the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class to monitor access patterns and move objects between access tiers. In S3 Intelligent-Tiering there are no retrieval charges, and no additional tiering charges apply when objects are moved between access tiers.

claim: Moving data into any storage class with PUT, COPY or a lifecycle rule costs a per-request ingest (transition) charge, so a transition of many small objects can cost more than it saves.
question: Does a lifecycle transition cost anything by itself?

values.display: per-request ingest charges
Consider the ingest or transition cost before moving objects into any storage class

qualifiers.condition: PUT, COPY or lifecycle transition into a storage class

evidence.quote: There are per-request ingest charges when using PUT, COPY, or lifecycle rules to move data into any S3 storage class. Consider the ingest or transition cost before moving objects into any storage class.

claim: LIST requests on any storage class are charged at the S3 Standard PUT, COPY and POST rate; DELETE and CANCEL requests are free.
question: Which S3 request types are free, and how are LIST requests charged?

values.display: DELETE and CANCEL requests are free
LIST requests for any storage class are charged at the same rate as S3 Standard PUT, COPY, and POST requests

evidence.quote: LIST requests for any storage class are charged at the same rate as S3 Standard PUT, COPY, and POST requests. DELETE and CANCEL requests are free.

claim: A retrieval charge applies on GET for S3 Standard-IA, S3 One Zone-IA and S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval; for S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive the retrieval is paid as part of the restore request.
question: Which storage classes charge for retrieval, and when is the charge taken?

values.display: S3 Standard – Infrequent Access, S3 One Zone – Infrequent Access, or S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
you pay for retrievals as a part of the restore request

qualifiers.scope: per GB retrieved, by storage class

evidence.quote: You pay for retrievals when you GET an object stored in the S3 Standard – Infrequent Access, S3 One Zone – Infrequent Access, or S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval storage classes. When you restore an archive from the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage classes, you pay for retrievals as a part of the restore request.

claim: While a restored archive is available, you pay for both the archived object (at its Glacier class rate) and the temporary restored copy, which is charged at the S3 Standard storage rate for the number of days you choose.
question: What do you pay for while a Glacier object is restored?

values.display: paying for both the archive
charged at the S3 Standard storage rate for a duration of time you choose

qualifiers.scope: per restored object, S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive

evidence.quote: When you restore an archive, you are paying for both the archive (charged at the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive rate) and a copy, accessible with GET using the same object key, that you restored temporarily (charged at the S3 Standard storage rate for a duration of time you choose).

claim: Data transferred into Amazon S3 from the internet is free.
question: Does uploading to S3 over the internet cost data transfer?

values.display: Data transferred in from the internet

evidence.quote: You pay for all bandwidth into and out of Amazon S3, except for the following:
Data transferred in from the internet.

claim: Data transferred out from Amazon S3 to Amazon CloudFront is free, which is one reason to put CloudFront in front of a bucket that serves many downloads.
question: Does S3 charge data transfer out when CloudFront fetches from the bucket?

values.display: Data transferred out to Amazon CloudFront

evidence.quote: You pay for all bandwidth into and out of Amazon S3, except for the following:
Data transferred out to Amazon CloudFront (CloudFront).

claim: Data transferred from an S3 bucket to any AWS service in the same Region is free, including to a different account in that Region; so is transfer between S3 buckets in the same Region.
question: Does an EC2 instance pay data transfer to read from an S3 bucket in its own Region?

values.display: Data transferred from an Amazon S3 bucket to any AWS service(s) within the same AWS Region as the S3 bucket
Data transferred between S3 buckets in the same AWS Region

qualifiers.condition: destination in the same AWS Region

evidence.quote: Data transferred from an Amazon S3 bucket to any AWS service(s) within the same AWS Region as the S3 bucket (including to a different account in the same AWS Region).
Data transferred between S3 buckets in the same AWS Region.

claim: The first 100GB per month of data transferred out to the internet is free, aggregated across all AWS services and Regions (except China and GovCloud).
question: How much data transfer out to the internet is free each month?

values.display: first 100GB per month
values.spoken: the first one hundred gigabytes per month

qualifiers.scope: per account, per month, aggregated across all AWS services and Regions

evidence.quote: Data transferred out to the internet for the first 100GB per month, aggregated across all AWS Services and Regions (except China and GovCloud)

claim: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up internet transfers between a client and one bucket; its price depends on the edge location used and is added on top of normal data transfer pricing.
question: How is S3 Transfer Acceleration billed?

values.display: based on the AWS edge location used
in addition to Data Transfer pricing

qualifiers.scope: per GB accelerated, per edge location

evidence.quote: S3 Transfer Acceleration accelerates internet transfers between the client and a single S3 bucket. Pricing is based on the AWS edge location used to accelerate your transfer. S3 Transfer Acceleration pricing is in addition to Data Transfer pricing.

claim: On each accelerated upload AWS checks whether Transfer Acceleration is likely to be faster than a regular transfer to the same Region; if not, that use is not charged and may bypass the acceleration system.
question: Do you pay for Transfer Acceleration when it would not be faster?

values.display: we will not charge for that use of S3 Transfer Acceleration for that transfer

qualifiers.condition: AWS determines the transfer is not likely to be faster than a regular transfer

evidence.quote: If we determine that it is not likely to be faster than a regular Amazon S3 transfer of the same object to the same destination AWS Region, we will not charge for that use of S3 Transfer Acceleration for that transfer, and may bypass the S3 Transfer Acceleration system for that upload.

claim: Transfer Acceleration optimizes transfer speed from anywhere in the world into a general purpose bucket: data enters at a CloudFront edge location and is routed to S3 over an optimized network path.
question: How does S3 Transfer Acceleration make long-distance uploads faster?

values.display: globally distributed edge locations in Amazon CloudFront
routed to Amazon S3 over an optimized network path

qualifiers.condition: Transfer Acceleration enabled on the bucket

evidence.quote: Transfer Acceleration is designed to optimize transfer speeds from across the world into S3 general purpose buckets. Transfer Acceleration takes advantage of the globally distributed edge locations in Amazon CloudFront. As the data arrives at an edge location, the data is routed to Amazon S3 over an optimized network path.

claim: Transfer Acceleration is the choice when customers upload to one central bucket from all over the world, or when you move gigabytes to terabytes across continents on a regular basis.
question: Which exam scenario points to S3 Transfer Acceleration rather than CloudFront or multipart upload?

values.display: upload to a centralized general purpose bucket from all over the world
gigabytes to terabytes of data on a regular basis across continents

evidence.quote: Your customers upload to a centralized general purpose bucket from all over the world.
You transfer gigabytes to terabytes of data on a regular basis across continents.

claim: AWS best practice is to use multipart upload for objects of 100 MB or larger instead of a single upload operation.
question: From what object size should you switch to multipart upload?

values.display: 100 MB or larger

qualifiers.condition: best practice, not a hard limit

evidence.quote: It's a best practice to use multipart upload for objects that are 100 MB or larger instead of uploading them in a single operation.

claim: With multipart upload you upload parts in parallel to improve throughput, and a failed part is retransmitted without affecting the other parts.
question: Why does multipart upload make large uploads faster and more resilient?

values.display: upload parts in parallel to improve throughput
retransmit that part without affecting other parts

evidence.quote: If transmission of any part fails, you can retransmit that part without affecting other parts.
**Improved throughput** – You can upload parts in parallel to improve throughput.

claim: After you start a multipart upload and upload parts, you pay for storage of those parts until you complete or stop the upload; only then does S3 free the parts and stop billing.
question: Why do incomplete multipart uploads cost money, and what stops the charge?

values.display: you must either complete or stop the multipart upload to stop incurring charges for storage of the uploaded parts

qualifiers.condition: a lifecycle rule can abort incomplete multipart uploads

evidence.quote: After you initiate a multipart upload and upload one or more parts, you must either complete or stop the multipart upload to stop incurring charges for storage of the uploaded parts. Only *after* you complete or stop a multipart upload will Amazon S3 free up the parts storage and stop billing you for the parts storage.

claim: Cross-Region Replication adds inter-Region data transfer out from S3 to each destination Region; S3 Replication Time Control adds an RTC data transfer charge and replication metrics billed like CloudWatch custom metrics.
question: What extra charges do CRR and Replication Time Control add?

values.display: inter-region Data Transfer OUT from S3 to each destination region
Replication Time Control Data Transfer charge and S3 Replication Metrics charges

qualifiers.scope: per GB replicated, Cross-Region Replication and Replication Time Control

evidence.quote: For CRR, you also pay for inter-region Data Transfer OUT from S3 to each destination region. When you use S3 Replication Time Control, you also pay a Replication Time Control Data Transfer charge and S3 Replication Metrics charges that are billed at the same rate as Amazon CloudWatch custom metrics.

claim: Live replication (CRR and SRR) copies only newly uploaded objects as they are written; S3 Batch Replication copies existing objects, as a managed S3 Batch Operations job.
question: Does turning on replication copy the objects that are already in the bucket?

values.display: automatically replicates newly uploaded objects as they are written to your bucket
S3 Batch Replication allows you to replicate existing objects

evidence.quote: While live replication like CRR and SRR automatically replicates newly uploaded objects as they are written to your bucket, S3 Batch Replication allows you to replicate existing objects. S3 Batch Replication is built using S3 Batch Operations to replicate objects as fully managed Batch Operations jobs.

claim: A Multi-Region Access Point adds a data routing cost per GB processed on top of the normal S3 request, storage, data transfer and replication charges.
question: What does a Multi-Region Access Point cost beyond normal S3 charges?

values.display: data routing cost for each gigabyte (GB) processed

qualifiers.scope: per GB routed through the Multi-Region Access Point
qualifiers.condition: requests routed within AWS; internet acceleration is an extra charge

evidence.quote: When you use an S3 Multi-Region Access Point to route requests within AWS, you pay a data routing cost for each gigabyte (GB) processed, as well as standard charges for S3 requests, storage, data transfer, and replication.

claim: S3 Multi-Region Access Points, built on AWS Global Accelerator, route each request over the AWS network to the lowest-latency copy of data that is replicated across several Regions, and can speed access by up to 60%.
question: What does a Multi-Region Access Point do for a data set replicated across Regions?

values.display: dynamically route your requests over the AWS network to the lowest latency copy of your data
up to 60%

qualifiers.condition: data sets replicated across multiple AWS Regions

evidence.quote: Amazon S3 Multi-Region Access Points accelerate performance by up to 60% when accessing data sets that are replicated across multiple AWS Regions. Based on AWS Global Accelerator, S3 Multi-Region Access Points consider factors like network congestion and the location of the requesting application to dynamically route your requests over the AWS network to the lowest latency copy of your data.

claim: Configure a bucket as Requester Pays when you want to share data but not pay the charges that other people's access to it creates; the requester then pays the request and data transfer cost.
question: When is a Requester Pays bucket the right answer?

values.display: share data but not incur charges associated with others accessing the data

evidence.quote: Typically, you want to configure your buckets as requester pays buckets if you wish to share data but not incur charges associated with others accessing the data.

As a bucket owner, if your bucket is configured to be a Requester Pays bucket, the requester pays all of the cost associated to the endpoint usage, including the cost for requests and data transfer cost associated to both the bucket and the Multi-Region Access Point.

claim: S3 Intelligent-Tiering is the class for data with unknown, changing or unpredictable access patterns, independent of object size or retention period, and can be the default class for almost any workload.
question: Which storage class do you choose when the access pattern is unknown or changes?

values.display: unknown, changing, or unpredictable access patterns
the default storage class for virtually any workload

evidence.quote: S3 Intelligent-Tiering is the ideal storage class for data with unknown, changing, or unpredictable access patterns, independent of object size or retention period. You can use S3 Intelligent-Tiering as the default storage class for virtually any workload, especially data lakes, data analytics, new applications, and user-generated content.

claim: An object smaller than 128 KB in S3 Intelligent-Tiering is not monitored and not eligible for auto-tiering; it always stays in the Frequent Access tier.
question: Why does S3 Intelligent-Tiering not save money on many small objects?

values.display: less than 128 KB
values.spoken: less than one hundred twenty-eight kilobytes

values.display: always stored in the Frequent Access tier

evidence.quote: If the size of an object is less than 128 KB, it is not monitored and not eligible for auto-tiering. Smaller objects are always stored in the Frequent Access tier.

claim: Activate the optional Archive Access and Deep Archive Access tiers of S3 Intelligent-Tiering only if the application can read asynchronously: an object in those tiers must first be restored with RestoreObject.
question: When should you not turn on the Intelligent-Tiering archive tiers?

values.display: only if your objects can be accessed asynchronously
first restore the object by using RestoreObject

qualifiers.scope: S3 Intelligent-Tiering, Archive Access and Deep Archive Access tiers

evidence.quote: Activate the Archive Access and Deep Archive Access tiers only if your objects can be accessed asynchronously by your application. If the object that you are retrieving is stored in the Archive Access or Deep Archive Access tiers, first restore the object by using `RestoreObject`.
